title: Federal System
description: Explore Nepal's federal system with provinces, local governments, and power distribution.

sections.title: Understanding Federalism in Nepal
sections.content: Nepal adopted federalism through the Constitution of 2015, transforming from a unitary state to a federal democratic republic. Federalism distributes power between the federal government, seven provinces, and 753 local governments. This system aims to ensure inclusive development, local autonomy, and equitable resource distribution while maintaining national unity.
keyPoints: Transition from unitary to federal system
Three levels of government: federal, provincial, local
Focus on inclusive and equitable development

sections.title: Three Levels of Government
sections.content: The Constitution establishes three levels of government with distinct powers and responsibilities. The federal government handles national defense, foreign policy, and citizenship. Provincial governments manage education, health, and internal security within their territories. Local governments focus on basic services, local infrastructure, and community development programs.
keyPoints: Federal level: defense, foreign policy, currency
Provincial level: education, health, internal security
Local level: basic services, local infrastructure
Clear division prevents overlap and conflict

sections.title: Seven Provinces of Nepal
sections.content: Nepal is divided into seven provinces, each with its own government, assembly, and chief minister. The provinces are: Koshi, Madhesh, Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini, Karnali, and Sudurpashchim. Each province has the authority to make laws on provincial matters, collect certain taxes, and implement development programs suited to their regional needs and priorities.
keyPoints: Each province has its own government and assembly
Provincial assemblies make laws on provincial matters
Provinces can address regional development needs

sections.title: Local Government Structure
sections.content: Local governments comprise municipalities and rural municipalities, each governed by elected councils. There are 293 municipalities and 460 rural municipalities across Nepal. Local governments have significant autonomy in delivering basic services like education, healthcare, water supply, and sanitation. They also have taxation powers and can implement local development projects based on community needs.

sections.title: Fiscal Federalism and Revenue Sharing
sections.content: Fiscal federalism defines how revenue powers and transfers are structured—assigning taxes, sharing national revenue, and providing equalization grants to address disparities. Transparent formulas and predictable transfers underpin stable service delivery and trust among tiers.
keyPoints: Assignment of tax bases to levels

sections.title: Intergovernmental Coordination
sections.content: Councils, forums, and joint committees facilitate negotiation over overlapping mandates—especially in health, education, and infrastructure—reducing duplication and conflict. Data sharing platforms enhance policy coherence.

sections.title: Devolution Challenges
sections.content: Capacity gaps, uneven resource endowments, and administrative fragmentation can slow effective devolution. Targeted training, performance benchmarking, and digital systems help strengthen local governance maturity.

sections.title: Service Delivery Impact
sections.content: Closer proximity to citizens enables tailored programs in agriculture, sanitation, and primary education. Measuring outcomes (coverage, quality, satisfaction) informs iterative improvements and equitable scaling.

sections.title: Comparative Perspective on Federalism
sections.content: Nepal’s relatively recent transition places it in a formative consolidation phase compared with long-established federations. Emphasis on inclusion and geographic balance distinguishes its model. Learning networks and international benchmarking accelerate institutional learning.

sections.title: Historical Context of Federal Transition
sections.content: Adoption of federalism followed demands for equitable representation, post‑conflict restructuring, and decentralization to address historical marginalization. Negotiated settlements embedded multi‑level governance commitments.

sections.title: Practical Implementation Dynamics
sections.content: Rollout requires sequencing legal frameworks, fiscal transfers, human resource deployment, and digital registries. Capacity mapping and staged devolution mitigate disruption of essential services.

sections.title: Adaptive Challenges
sections.content: Overlapping functional lists, variable provincial capacity, and uneven revenue bases create coordination friction. Standardized reporting templates and peer‑learning forums accelerate convergence.

sections.title: Future Outlook
sections.content: Next steps emphasize results‑oriented intergovernmental compacts, data harmonization, outcome benchmarking across provinces, and inclusive fiscal equalization refinement.

sections.title: Case Study: Applying Concepts
sections.content: A practical scenario demonstrates how principles from "Federal System" operate in real life. Consider a local authority decision challenged for compliance with constitutional norms. Analyze actors involved, legal basis, and remedy pathways to understand implementation dynamics.
keyPoints: Reflect on lessons for future decisions

sections.title: Implementation Gaps and Challenges
sections.content: Even with strong legal and policy frameworks, realizing "Federal System" can face capacity, coordination, and resource constraints. Data quality and awareness gaps may slow progress and produce uneven outcomes across regions.
